Calculate Huff-model Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (Huff-2SFCA) scores

Source: R/03-spax_e2sfca.R
spax_huff2sfca.Rd

This experimental function implements a floating catchment area method in which the selection weights of spax_3sfca are replaced by a Huff selection probability, following Luo (2014). The probability that an origin selects a facility uses the attractiveness of the facilities and a distance decay, so a more attractive facility gathers a larger share of the demand at each origin.

Usage

spax_huff2sfca(
  demand,
  supply,
  distance,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 30),
  selection_params = decay_params,
  attractiveness = NULL,
  alpha = 1,
  id_col = NULL,
  supply_cols = NULL,
  indicator_names = NULL,
  snap = FALSE
)

Arguments

demand

SpatRaster representing spatial distribution of demand, or a named list of single-layer SpatRasters, one per demand group (see "Demand groups"). A multi-layer SpatRaster is refused. Demand must be finite and nonnegative (use NA for unknown) unless snap = TRUE, which ignores other cells.

supply

vector, matrix, or data.frame containing supply capacity values

distance

SpatRaster stack of travel times/distances to facilities. With demand groups, either one stack shared by every group or a list of stacks named by the groups (for example one per travel mode); the stacks of all groups must name the same facilities in the same order and have the same geometry (reorder with x[[names(first)]]).

decay_params

List of parameters for the decay weights used in both steps (with demand groups, one list shared by every group, or a list of such lists named by the groups):

  • method: "gaussian", "exponential", "power" or "binary", a custom decay function, or a kernel declared with decay_kernel. Weights must be finite where the distance is finite, so power decay needs a positive minimum distance

  • sigma: decay parameter controlling the rate of distance decay

  • Additional parameters passed to custom decay functions

selection_params

List of parameters, in the form of decay_params, for the decay weights that the selection weights are built from. The default is decay_params, so one decay both weights distance and selects facilities; give a different list to select with another decay. Its weights must also be finite where the distance is finite. With demand groups, shared or a list named by the groups; a group whose selection list is identical to its decay list reuses the decay weights.

attractiveness

Numeric vector of facility attractiveness with one finite, nonnegative value per facility, shared by the demand groups. A named vector is matched to the layer names of distance (with groups, of the first group's stack); an unnamed vector follows the order of the layers. The default, NULL, uses the supply measure, which requires supply to have exactly one measure; give attractiveness when it has several.

alpha

Nonnegative number: the exponent of attractiveness in the selection probability. With alpha = 0 attractiveness has no effect and the result equals spax_3sfca.

id_col

Character; column name for facility IDs if supply is a data.frame

supply_cols

Character vector; names of supply columns if supply is a data.frame

indicator_names

Character vector; custom names for output accessibility layers

snap

Logical; if TRUE enable fast computation mode (default = FALSE)

Value

A spax object (see spax_e2sfca) whose type is "Huff-2SFCA". Its parameters are the named list decay_params, selection_params, attractiveness (the numeric vector in the order of the distance layers, named by facility ID) and alpha.

Details

Write \(D_i\) for the demand at origin \(i\), \(S_j\) for the supply of facility \(j\), \(a_j\) for its attractiveness, \(W_{ij}\) for the decay weights from decay_params and \(T_{ij}\) for the decay weights from selection_params. The two are the same weights when selection_params is identical to decay_params.

  • Selection probabilities: \(G_{ij} = a_j^\alpha T_{ij} / \sum_k a_k^\alpha T_{ik}\).

  • Ratio of facility \(j\): \(R_j = S_j / \sum_i D_i W_{ij} G_{ij}\).

  • Accessibility of origin \(i\): \(A_i = \sum_j R_j W_{ij} G_{ij}\).

The structure is that of spax_3sfca, to which the method reduces when alpha = 0 (a facility with zero attractiveness then counts as 1, since \(0^0 = 1\)). Both steps use the kernel \(K_{ij} = W_{ij} G_{ij}\), and the result equals compute_access(demand, supply, demand_weights = K, access_weights = K) with K = W * calc_choice(T, attractiveness, alpha). A facility with zero attractiveness is never selected when alpha is positive. There is no demand_normalize argument: the selection probabilities already divide the demand of each origin among the facilities.

The probabilities are normalized over every facility with a positive weight at the origin, however far away it is. To restrict the selection to a catchment, set the travel times beyond the limit to NA or Inf before calling the function, or use a decay method that is zero beyond it, for example method = "binary" in selection_params.

Because both steps use the same kernel, the scores conserve supply: the sum of \(D_i A_i\) over the origins with demand and a score equals the total supply of the facilities that gather demand (\(\sum_i D_i K_{ij} > 0\)). A facility that gathers no demand has a ratio of zero. Several supply measures give independent accessibility layers that share one attractiveness.

Demand groups

Give demand as a named list of single-layer rasters (for example age bands) to let several groups compete for the same facilities. The names are the group IDs: unique, non-empty, not "all" and without a .; all rasters need the same geometry. A multi-layer raster is not taken as groups.

Step 1 sums, over all groups, the demand that reaches each facility, with the demand weights of each group; step 2 gives each group its own accessibility from the shared ratios, with its own weights. The result has one layer per group, and an overall layer <measure>.all: the average of the group scores weighted by the demand of the cell. A group with demand in a cell that its travel cannot reach counts with accessibility 0 in the overall layer; the overall layer is NA where any group's demand is missing or the total demand is 0. With one group the group layer equals the ungrouped result.

decay_params and distance (and selection_params of spax_3sfca() and spax_huff2sfca(), threshold of spax_2sfca()) are each either shared by every group or given per group. An argument is per group when it is a list (for threshold, a named numeric vector) whose names are the group IDs, in any order; names that match only some of the groups are refused. Any other value is shared and checked as for one group. Pass a shared distance as one object, so that it is read once. A plain-function decay builds a whole in-memory weight raster for each group. demand_normalize, indicator_names, id_col, supply_cols and the attractiveness of spax_huff2sfca() are shared.

References

Luo, J. (2014). Integrating the Huff model and floating catchment area methods to analyze spatial access to healthcare services. Transactions in GIS, 18(3), 436-448. doi:10.1111/tgis.12096

Wan, N., Zou, B., & Sternberg, T. (2012). A three-step floating catchment area method for analyzing spatial access to health services. International Journal of Geographical Information Science, 26(6), 1073-1089. doi:10.1080/13658816.2011.624987

See also

spax_3sfca for selection weights that do not depend on attractiveness, spax_e2sfca, spax_m2sfca, compute_access, calc_decay, calc_choice and decay_kernel. vignette("fca-methods", package = "spax") compares the FCA methods on the Cornwall data.

Examples

# Load example data
library(terra)
library(sf)

# Cornwall population grid and travel time to each GP practice
pop_rast <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")

# Drop geometry for supply data
gp <- cornwall_gp |> st_drop_geometry()

# Attractiveness defaults to the supply measure (GP FTE excluding trainees)
result <- spax_huff2sfca(
  demand = pop_rast,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
plot(result$accessibility, main = "GP Accessibility (Huff-2SFCA)")


# Another attractiveness, named by practice, with a stronger effect
result_gp <- spax_huff2sfca(
  demand = pop_rast,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  attractiveness = setNames(gp$gp_fte, gp$practice), # all GPs
  alpha = 2,
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

# Plot both for comparison
plot(c(result$accessibility, result_gp$accessibility),
  main = c("Attractiveness = supply", "All GPs, alpha = 2")
)
